plain: It's a sketchbook that lives inside the browser. There you draw how you want your website or app to look before it exists: the rectangle where the photo will go, the orange button, the price right below it. Figma doesn't build anything, and it doesn't need to: it's the blueprint, like the one an architect draws on paper before anyone touches a brick. And that blueprint, turned into a simple screenshot, is what you're going to show the AI so it can build the house.

account.free: Yes, there's a free plan, and it's more than enough for what you're going to do. It's called 'Starter', costs 0 dollars, and doesn't ask for a card. It gives you three shared design files, three FigJam whiteboards, and personal drafts; free-plan files are limited to three pages each. Anyone you send the link to can view it without an account. The big catch: the free plan's version history only keeps the last 30 days, so what you broke five weeks ago isn't coming back. The paid plan for a single person, 'Professional', runs around 15-20 dollars per person per month depending on whether you pay annually or monthly. Figma reorganized pricing and seat types in 2025 and the numbers move around: check the exact figure at figma.com/pricing before paying anything, don't trust the one I give you.
steps: Go to figma.com. In the center there's a button that says 'Get started for free'. You can sign in with Google in one click, or with email and password. If you use email, you get sent a message with a 'Verify email' button: you can't continue until you click it. Check your spam folder, it often lands there.
Choose the free plan, which is hidden

After signing up you get asked two or three questions ('What brings you to Figma?') and then a plans screen appears with 'Professional' highlighted and a free trial. Scroll down and look for the word 'Starter': that's the free one, and it's always the least eye-catching option on the screen. If at any point it asks for a card number, you've wandered into the paid trial: go back.
Download the desktop app (recommended, not required)

Go to figma.com/downloads and click 'Download for Windows'. It works the same as the browser version, but uses less memory and, importantly, can use the fonts installed on your own computer. In the browser you'll only see the fonts Figma ships by default.
Create your first file and give it a real name

In the left column click 'Drafts' and then the '+' or 'New' button top right; choose 'Design file'. An infinite gray canvas opens. Top left it says 'Untitled': double-click it and type something like 'dental-clinic-site-v1'. Two weeks from now you'll have four files, and if you don't do this now none of them will be named after what they contain.
Draw the first frame, which is a whole screen

Press the F key. A panel on the right shows a list of ready-made sizes: 'Desktop' with the 1440 x 1024 option, and 'Phone' with sizes like 390 x 844. Click one and a white rectangle appears on the canvas. That white rectangle is one screen of your website. Everything you draw has to fall inside it.
Confirm it saves itself and find the share button

There's no Ctrl+S: Figma saves every change to its server as you make it. To go back, menu 'File' then 'Version history'. Top right is the blue 'Share' button; inside it, the option 'Anyone with the link' makes your file public to anyone with the address. Leave it on 'Only people invited' while you're still testing.
account.warning: None of this lives on your computer: delete a file and it goes to Figma's trash, and from there it can be emptied for good, with no way back. And on the free plan, history only goes back 30 days. Before redoing a screen you already liked, duplicate it (Ctrl+D) and work on the copy: costs two seconds and saves you an afternoon.

first: Create a file and name it after the project, not 'test'. Inside it, a single screen: the most important one, the one someone sees when they arrive for the first time.
Press F and pick 'Phone' (about 390 x 844). Draw the mobile version FIRST. It's narrower, forces you to decide what's extra, and going from mobile to desktop is easy; the other way around, it isn't.
Draw everything in gray: rectangles with R for photos and buttons, text with T. No colors, no shadows, no pretty fonts. You're deciding WHAT goes where and in what order, not how nice it looks.

Write the real text: the actual headline, the actual price in dollars, the button with the real word ('Book now', not 'Button'). Placeholder text lies about how much space things take up, and the AI will copy it exactly as written.

Select the whole frame by clicking its name (the gray text right above the white rectangle), press Ctrl+Shift+C, and paste it into the AI's chat with Ctrl+V. If the image shows up, you now know the one truly essential thing about this tool.
shortcuts: F

Creates a frame, which is a screen. Press it and the right-hand panel offers ready-made sizes: 'Desktop' 1440 x 1024, 'Phone' 390 x 844, 'Tablet'. Everything you draw needs to be inside a frame: anything left loose on the canvas won't show up in the screenshot or get exported.
R and T (and V to go back, Esc to exit)

R draws a rectangle, T writes text. With those two keys you do 90% of a wireframe: a rectangle is a photo, a button, a card, or a bar. V gives you back the normal arrow for moving things, and Esc gets you out of whatever you're editing.
Spacebar + drag, and Ctrl + mouse wheel

Holding the spacebar while dragging moves the whole canvas without touching anything drawn. Ctrl plus the wheel zooms. Without this you end up accidentally moving a button across the map without understanding what happened.
Shift+2 and Shift+1
Shift+2 zooms in until the selection fills the screen. Shift+1 zooms out until the whole file is visible. You'll use these fifty times a day to jump from detail to overview and back.
Alt + drag

Duplicates whatever you drag and leaves the original where it was. It's making a card and pulling three identical copies out in one motion. Hold Shift too and the copy comes out perfectly aligned with the original.
Alt held down (without dragging)

Select something, hold Alt, and hover over something else: red numbers appear with the exact pixel distance between the two. That's how you discover one gap measures 23 and the one next to it 24, which is what makes a design look messy without knowing why.
Shift+A

Turns the selection into auto layout: elements arrange themselves in a row or column with equal spacing, and if you add one, the others make room. It's the closest thing to how a real website behaves, and it helps the AI understand your screenshot better.
Ctrl+Shift+C

Copy as PNG (image). This is THE shortcut of the whole course. Select the frame, press this, go to the AI's chat, and paste with Ctrl+V: your design's screenshot shows up in the message, clean, with no browser bars or Figma menus around it.
Ctrl+Shift+E

Opens 'Export' to save the image as a file. Useful when the AI tool won't let you paste and asks you to upload a file. In that panel, change '1x' to '2x': the image comes out at double resolution and the AI reads small text much better.
Ctrl+/

Opens the action search: type in English what you want to do ('export', 'component', 'flatten') and it runs it without you fighting through menus. Each result also shows its shortcut next to it, so it's the fastest way to learn the ones you're missing.
daily: One frame = one screen, and nothing loose on the canvas. If something's outside a frame, for practical purposes it doesn't exist: it won't show up in the screenshot, won't get exported, and the AI will never see it.

Gray first, color later. Draw the whole structure in grayscale and add color only once you're happy with the order of things. Nine out of ten ugly screens are ugly because of the order, not the color.

Name the important layers. In the left column, double-click on 'Rectangle 47' and type 'book-now-button'. When you hand the screenshot to the AI and say 'the book now button', you'll both be talking about the same thing.

Decide colors and type ONCE: two colors (one for text, one for accent), one typeface, and four font sizes. Write them down in a corner of the canvas. Every new screen comes from there, not from whatever you feel like that day.

Copy with Ctrl+Shift+C and paste into the AI's chat. That's the entire handoff: screenshot plus your explanation in English. There's no magic intermediate step, and anyone selling you one is selling smoke.
When the AI builds something, screenshot the result and put it next to the design, on the same canvas. Seeing them side by side shows you in two seconds what you'd never see jumping between windows.
Duplicate before redesigning: Ctrl+D on the frame and rename the copy 'v2'. That way you can show both to someone and decide, instead of trying to remember what the earlier one looked like.

templates.name: Free kits from the Figma Community (pre-drawn sketches and pieces)
templates.what: The Community is a public library of files other people have made and given away. Instead of drawing a dropdown menu or a calendar from scratch, you bring in a ready-made one and change it. For someone who isn't going to code, this is the difference between an afternoon and ten minutes to have a presentable blueprint. Watch out: there are free and paid files, and it's not always obvious at a glance.
templates.how: Go to figma.com/community. There's a search bar up top and some tabs: click 'Files' so you don't mix it up with plugins. In the price filter, check 'Free'. Search for these terms, which are the ones that work: 'wireframe kit', 'Material 3 Design Kit' (Google's official Android one), 'Apple Design Resources' or 'iOS' (Apple's official ones), 'Untitled UI' (one of the most-used free kits), and 'shadcn' (pieces that resemble the code the AI usually writes, so the result ends up closer to the drawing). On the file's page, top right, there's a blue button: it says 'Open in Figma' or 'Get a copy' / 'Duplicate'. Click it and a copy of YOUR OWN gets created in your drafts; the original never gets touched. Watch the free plan's limit: every copy you bring in counts as a file and you only have three. Inside the copy, go to the page called 'Components' or 'Cover', copy the piece you want with Ctrl+C, and paste it with Ctrl+V into your working file. The exact names of kits change over time: if one doesn't show up, search 'wireframe' or 'UI kit' and sort by 'Most popular'.
fill: The text on every button and headline the kit brings
Your real words: 'Book now', 'See pricing', your business name
The kit's accent color (almost always a blue)
Your color, the same on every screen
The sample photos
Gray rectangles with a note inside saying what photo goes there, until you have your own
The sections you're not going to use
Delete them. A kit brings 60 pieces and you need 8; the leftover ones confuse the AI when you hand it the screenshot
The kit's typeface
Swap for your own, if the kit uses one you don't have installed and you get the missing-font warning

templates.name: screen-map.txt: decide the screens before drawing anything
templates.what: A one-page document where you decide which screens you need, in what order, and what the important button on each one is. Takes fifteen minutes to fill in and prevents this course's most expensive mistake: spending three days drawing screens that weren't needed. It also works as your first message to the AI, because it explains the whole project before it sees a single image.
templates.how: Copy the text below into any notepad and save it alongside your project as screen-map.txt. Fill in everything [in brackets] and delete the brackets. Hard rule: four screens maximum to launch; everything else goes on the second-version list, where good ideas that would delay you two months need to wait. Once you have it, open your Figma file and create one frame per screen on the list, with the exact same name. If you'd rather see it drawn out, put it together in FigJam, Figma's whiteboard (free on the Starter plan): from your files screen, '+' button then 'FigJam board'; there you place one sticky note per screen and arrows between them to see the whole flow at a glance.
fill: [PROJECT NAME]
The real name of the business or idea
WHAT I SELL / WHAT I OFFER
One sentence, no adjectives: what you give, in exchange for what
WHO'S VISITING
Rough age, what device they're on, and how much of a hurry they're in
WHAT I WANT THEM TO DO
One single action. List three and you won't get any
Routes like /contact
The addresses you want to show up in the browser bar
templates.code:
SCREEN MAP — [PROJECT NAME]
Date: [MM/DD/YYYY]   Version: 1

WHAT I SELL / WHAT I OFFER (one sentence, no adjectives):
  [Example: bathroom remodels in Austin, quote within 24 hours]

WHO'S VISITING (one sentence):
  [Example: homeowner aged 40 to 65, on mobile, in a hurry]

WHAT I WANT THEM TO DO BEFORE LEAVING (one single thing):
  [Example: leave their phone number in the form]

--- SCREENS TO LAUNCH WITH (four max) ---

1. [Home]                   route [/]
   Sections top to bottom:
     - [Top bar]
     - [Hero: headline + button + photo]
     - [3 cards]
     - [Footer]
   Main button: [Get a quote]  ->  goes to [/contact]

2. [Work]                    route [/work]
   Sections: [grid of 6 photos with title and "from $X"]
   Main button: [View details]  ->  goes to [/work/one]

3. [Contact]                 route [/contact]
   Sections: [3-field form] + [thank-you message]
   Main button: [Send]

--- THE ONES EVERYONE ALWAYS FORGETS (check the ones you need) ---
   [ ] Thanks, we got your message
   [ ] No results / empty list
   [ ] Something went wrong, try again
   [ ] Loading
   [ ] Cookie notice + privacy page
   [ ] 404: this page doesn't exist

--- FOR VERSION TWO (don't draw these now) ---
   [Blog, customer area, card payment, search]

--- FRAME SIZES I'M GOING TO DRAW IN FIGMA ---
   Mobile:  390 x 844    (draw this one FIRST)
   Desktop: 1440 x 1024

templates.name: design.json: the spec sheet that goes with the screenshot
templates.what: The file you paste to the AI ALONGSIDE the screenshot. The image shows it the shape; this spec sheet gives it the exact data an image can't convey: the exact color code, the typeface name, the font sizes, what stacks on mobile, and which text is untouchable. With the screenshot alone, the AI gets the shape right and the details wrong; with both, it gets it right the first time far more often.
templates.how: Copy the block below into a text file called design.json and save it in your project folder. Now fill it in from Figma: click any element and look at the panel on the RIGHT. There you'll see the color in #RRGGBB format (click the little color swatch and copy it), the typeface name, the size in pixels, and the corner rounding ('Corner radius'). Get the spacing between sections by holding Alt and hovering between two elements. Once you have it, open the AI's chat, paste the file's content, paste the screenshot below it (Ctrl+Shift+C in Figma, Ctrl+V in the chat), and type your request in English. Keep it safe: every time you ask for a new screen, paste this same sheet again, and everything comes out with the same colors without you repeating yourself.
fill: The nine colors
The # codes you see in Figma's right-hand panel when selecting each element
The typeface and the five sizes
Whatever shows up in the 'Typography' section of the right-hand panel when selecting a text element
max_content_width_px and corner_radius_px
Your desktop frame's width and your cards' 'Corner radius' value
The list of screens and their sections
Copied from your screen-map.txt, plus whatever you've drawn since
on_click
Where each button leads. Leave it out and the AI will build a button that goes nowhere

templates.name: styles.css: your Figma colors turned into one file
templates.what: The bridge between the design and what gets built. It's a file with your colors, your font sizes, and your spacing written once and named. You tell the AI 'use this file and don't invent colors' and every screen comes out the same. And the day you want to swap the orange for a green, you change one line instead of hunting the orange down in forty places. You don't need to understand what it says: just swap out what's in brackets.
templates.how: Copy the block into a file called styles.css inside your project folder. Replace each [bracketed] value with what you see in Figma's right-hand panel and delete the brackets. Then tell the AI: 'here's my styles.css, link it in the HTML and use ONLY these variables; don't write loose colors or sizes, and if you need a new one, ask me first'. The classes below already give you the pieces you end up drawing every time: .button, .card, .container, .grid (which stacks on its own on mobile), and .photo-placeholder (the gray rectangle for photos you don't have yet). The dark mode block only activates if the visitor's phone is set to dark; if you don't want it, delete the whole block starting with @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark).
fill: --color-accent
Your main color, the one on the important button. One only, not three
--font
The exact typeface name as it appears in Figma, for example Inter or Poppins
--text-xl through --text-xs
Your design's five font sizes, from the big headline to small text
--max-width and --radius
Your desktop frame's width and your cards' corner rounding
The dark mode block's colors
Only if you want dark mode. If not, delete the whole block

errors: 'Upgrade to create more files' or a warning that you've hit the Starter plan's limit, when creating a new file

You've hit the three design files the free plan gives you, almost always from bringing in copies from the Community. Don't pay for this yet: go into 'Recents', right-click files you no longer use, and choose 'Move to trash'. Before deleting a kit, copy and paste into your working file whatever pieces you want to keep.
Warning bar at the top: 'Reconnecting...' or 'Connection lost'

Your internet connection dropped. Figma doesn't work without it because the file lives on their server. Leave the tab OPEN: once the connection comes back, it syncs the last few minutes of changes. Close it abruptly while that's showing and you can lose your last few actions.
'Missing font' or a warning like 'N fonts are missing from this file'

The file uses a typeface your computer doesn't have, typical when duplicating a Community file. Text shows up in a different font and out of place. Two fixes: click 'Replace font' in the warning and pick Inter, which Figma always includes; or install the font on your system and use Figma's desktop app, because the browser can't see your computer's fonts.
You can't move anything and it says 'View only' or 'Can view' at the top

You're inside someone else's file, with permission to look and nothing else. It's not broken. Menu 'File' then 'Duplicate', or the 'Get a copy' button if you came from the Community: that creates your own editable copy. You will never be able to edit someone else's original no matter how much you insist.
You press Ctrl+Shift+C, go to the AI's chat, paste, and no image shows up

Almost always you had nothing selected, or you had an empty layer selected. Go back to Figma, click the frame's NAME (the small gray text right above the white rectangle), confirm the whole frame gets outlined in blue, and repeat. If it still won't paste, use Ctrl+Shift+E, set '2x' and 'PNG' in the export panel, click 'Export', and upload the file to the chat by hand.
The AI builds something that doesn't resemble your design: changes the order, uses filler text, invents sections

The screenshot alone isn't enough. It's missing context: what each thing is, where each button leads, which text is real. Restart the message, pasting your design.json first, then the image, then the sentence 'the text in the image is real, copy it exactly; don't add any section that isn't in the image'. And give it ONE screen per message, not five at once.
You export the image and the background comes out as a gray checkerboard

That checkerboard means transparent: your frame has no fill color. The AI will see a strange background and might build the page with a transparent background. Select the frame and, in the right-hand panel, under 'Fill', click the '+' and set it to white (#FFFFFF).
You move an element inside a group and everything else jumps around, or it won't let you drag it where you want

That group has auto layout turned on: it arranges its children on its own, in a row or column, and doesn't allow manual placement. That's what you want 90% of the time. To change the order, drag the layer in the left-hand list. To change the gap, use the number between the arrow icons in the right-hand panel. And if you genuinely need manual placement, select the group and press Shift+Alt+A to remove auto layout. Related note: if you see the word 'Mixed' in the right panel where a number should go, you have several things selected with different values; typing over it applies the same value to all of them at once.

prompts.name: Turn a screenshot of your design into a working website (the core handoff prompt)
prompts.prompt: I'm sending you a screenshot of a design I made in Figma. I want you to turn it into a website that actually works, not an approximation. Before writing a single line of code, describe to me in a list what you see in the image: how many sections there are top to bottom, what each one contains, and which elements are clickable. If something in the image isn't clear, ask me instead of guessing. Once I confirm the list is correct, build the page with [HTML and CSS in a single file / React and Tailwind / whatever my project uses]. Rules you can't skip: keep the section order exactly as it is in the screenshot; use only these colors [PASTE THE COLOR CODES HERE, for example #1A1A1A for text and #FF6B35 for the button]; the typeface is [FONT NAME] and, if it's not available, use something similar and tell me. The text visible in the screenshot is real: copy it letter for letter, don't replace it with placeholder text or translate it. Where there are photos, leave a gray rectangle of the right size with a note inside saying what image goes there. The page needs to look good on a 375-pixel-wide phone: columns stack one under the other and buttons are at least 44 pixels tall, so they can be tapped with a finger. When you're done, tell me in three lines what you assumed and what I need to check.

prompts.name: Pull the colors, sizes, and spacing out of the design into reusable variables
prompts.prompt: I'm sending you a screenshot of my Figma design and, below it, the list of colors and font sizes I copied by hand from the right-hand panel: [PASTE THE COLOR CODES, THE SIZES IN PIXELS, AND THE TYPEFACE NAME HERE]. Turn this into a single variables file I can use across the whole project, so every screen we build from now on comes out with the same colors and the same measurements without me having to repeat myself each time. Do it like this. First, list the colors and name them by their FUNCTION, never by their color: background, soft background, text, soft text, accent, text on accent, border, error, and success. The reason is practical: if I swap the orange for a green tomorrow, I don't want to hunt down the word orange across forty files. Second, do the same with font sizes, spacing between elements, and corner rounding, but narrow each one to a short scale of five or six values at most; if my design has fifteen different spacing values, group them and tell me which ones you rounded. Third, write the result as [CSS variables inside :root / a tokens.json file / Tailwind config], complete and ready to paste, no half-finished parts or ellipses. Add the dark mode version if it makes sense. Finally, tell me which of my color combinations doesn't meet the minimum contrast for comfortable reading, and what value you'd fix it with. End with two sentences explaining how I use the file.

prompts.name: Decide which screens you need BEFORE opening Figma
prompts.prompt: I'm going to build [DESCRIBE YOUR PROJECT IN ONE SENTENCE: for example, a website for an Austin dental clinic that wants people to book appointments without calling]. Before I start drawing in Figma I want to know which screens I actually need and what goes on each one, so I don't draw things I don't need or discover halfway through that I'm missing half of it. My ideal customer is [WHO: rough age, what they're looking for, what device they're on, how much of a hurry they're in]. The one thing I want that person to do before leaving is [THE SPECIFIC ACTION: book an appointment, buy something, leave their email]. Give me the list of screens ranked by importance and, for each one, tell me: the name, its purpose in a single sentence, the sections it has top to bottom, what the main button is, and where it leads when clicked. Clearly mark which are essential for launch and which can wait for a second version, because I want to start with three or four screens, not fifteen. Also tell me which screens usually get forgotten in this kind of project: the thank-you-after-submitting one, the empty-list one, the error one, the loading one, the cookie notice, and the page-not-found one. Don't write any code yet: this is just the blueprint. End by recommending what frame size I should use in Figma to draw this, and why that one and not another.

prompts.name: Get your design critiqued before spending time building it
prompts.prompt: I'm sending you a screenshot of a screen I just drew in Figma. Don't build it yet: I want you to critique it, first as if you were the person who's going to use it and then as if you were the one who has to code it. Context: it's the [WHAT IT'S FOR] screen of [TYPE OF BUSINESS], and the person who'll see it is [WHO: age, device they're on, how much of a hurry they're in]. Answer in this order. One: what's the very first thing that catches the eye of someone looking at the screen for three seconds, and does that match what I want them to do, which is [THE ACTION]. Two: which elements are extra, repeated, or competing with each other for attention. Three: what's missing that's going to show once this is real, meaning long text that's going to break the box, the loading state, the empty-list state, the error state, and what it looks like if the user isn't signed in. Four: what breaks when this is viewed on a 375-pixel-wide phone. Five: whether there's any text with insufficient contrast or any clickable area too small for a finger. Rank the problems from most to least serious and, for each one, give me the specific fix I need to make in Figma, with numbers, not generic advice. Ten points maximum. Be harsh: I'd rather hear it now than after building it.

prompts.name: Close the gap between what you drew and what the AI built (two screenshots)
prompts.prompt: I'm sending you two images. The first is my design made in Figma. The second is a screenshot of what got built with the code you gave me. They don't match closely enough and I want to close that gap. Compare them and give me a list of the real differences you see, ranked from most noticeable to least: spacing between sections, font sizes, colors, alignment, border thickness, element order, and things that are outright missing. Ignore differences that come from the browser screenshot having a different window width than my Figma frame, but tell me if you think that's the main cause. For each difference, tell me which part of the code needs touching and give me the corrected piece ready to paste, saying which file it goes in and what exact text it replaces. My design's exact specs are: colors [PASTE THE CODES], typeface [NAME] at sizes [LIST OF SIZES], and the margin between sections is [NUMBER] pixels. If a difference can't be reproduced exactly because that's not how a browser works, tell me clearly and propose the closest alternative instead of staying quiet about it. Important: don't rebuild the whole page. I want small, localized changes, so I don't break what's already working.

words: Frame
The rectangle that represents ONE screen. It's the only container that matters: whatever's inside shows up in the screenshot, whatever's outside doesn't. Created with the F key.
Canvas
The infinite gray background where your frames float. No edges or limits: you can have thirty screens scattered across it, like papers on a very large table.
Layer
Every single thing you draw is a layer, and the left column is the list of all of them, nested inside each other. Whatever's higher on the list shows up in front.
Auto layout
Makes a group of elements arrange themselves, in a row or column, always with the same gap between them. Add one and the others make room. This is how real websites behave.
Component and instance
The component is the original of a piece you repeat (a button, a card); every copy is an instance. Change the original and every copy changes at once. Useful once you have many screens.
Wireframe
The gray drawing, no colors or photos, that only decides WHAT goes where and in what order. It's the phase you should spend the most time on, and where almost everyone spends the least.
Mockup
The wireframe with colors, typography, and photos already in place: what it'll really look like. This is what you hand the AI when you want the result to resemble the final thing, not the skeleton.
Prototype
Linking screens with arrows so clicking a button jumps to another and you can pretend to use it. Useful for showing someone; not needed for the AI to build it.
Plugin
An add-on that does something specific inside Figma: filling in with fake text, pulling out the color list, inserting icons. Installed from the Community and opened with right-click, 'Plugins'.
Export at 2x
Saving the image at double the size you see. It weighs more, but reads much better, so the AI can tell apart the small text in your screenshot instead of guessing it.
matters: Draw before asking the AI for anything. Open the chat with no blueprint and the AI will fill the gaps with what it thinks you want, and you'll spend the afternoon correcting in writing things you'd have solved in ten minutes by moving two rectangles. A twenty-minute gray wireframe is worth more than two hours of 'no, the button lower down'.

Real frames and named layers. The AI reads your screenshot as an image: the clearer the hierarchy (frame, sections inside, elements inside), the better it interprets it. And when you tell it 'move up the book now button', you need that thing to actually be called that somewhere. With forty layers named 'Rectangle 12' you won't understand each other, not even you and yourself a week from now.

Decide colors and typography once, at the start, and don't touch them again. Two colors, one font, four font sizes. Improvise on every screen and you'll end up with seven different blues, the AI will copy all of them, and your site will look built by seven people who don't talk to each other. Fixing it later means going through every screen by hand.

Mobile first, not as an afterthought. Most people are going to arrive from their phone. Design for a wide screen and then try to squeeze it in, and it breaks: three-word headlines take up four lines, tables spill over, and buttons end up too small for a finger. The other way around, from mobile to desktop, all you have to do is add breathing room.
ignore: Prototypes and animations (the 'Prototype' tab in the right-hand panel). Linking screens with arrows and making pretty transitions is fun and adds absolutely nothing to the handoff to the AI: a screenshot of a still screen tells it the same thing. Once your site is working, you'll have the real prototype anyway.

Components, variants, libraries, and shared styles. All of that solves the problem of keeping fifty screens consistent, and you're going to have four. Copy and paste with Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V works perfectly well until you start changing the same thing in more than five places; that day, and not before, you learn components.

'Dev Mode' and the code Figma writes on its own. The CSS it generates is meant for a programmer who knows what to keep; pasted as-is it gives odd results, with fixed positions that break on mobile. It also usually needs a paid seat. Your path is the screenshot plus the prompt in English, which works better and costs nothing.
